sources.classification: labelled from the task code, 2026-11-12 (synthetic data: dataset_samples not stated)

measurements.source: Lambda, github.com/lambdal/deeplearning-benchmark, commit aa5addb6 (2025-12-17), pytorch/pytorch-train-throughput-fp32.csv, column resnet50 (training throughput, images/s), single-GPU rows run with batch 640 (pytorch/pytorch-train-bs-fp32.csv): 'A100 80GB SXM4' 1066; 'A100 80GB PCIe' 1014; 'H100 80GB PCIe Gen5' 1197, 'LambdaCloud H100 80GB PCIe Gen5' 1182; 'H100 80GB SXM5' 1753, 'Dell H100 80GB SXM5' 1893, 'DellTexas H100 80GB SXM5' 1893, 'SMC H100 80GB SXM5' 1893, '1CC H100 80GB SXM5' 1898, 'RAIDZ1 H100 80GB SXM5' 1894
measurements.date: measurement dates are not in the CSV; repository snapshot 2025-12-17
measurements.hardware: Lambda's systems as named in the rows; NVIDIA NGC PyTorch container (version not recorded per row), LambdaLabsML/DeepLearningExamples branch lambda/benchmark
measurements.anchor_compute_sec_note: training work / published throughput of the anchor: 2 epochs x 100 iterations x batch 640 = 128000 images; / 1066.0 images/s. The benchmark's throughput covers the training steps: start-up and validation are outside it
measurements.compute_ratio_note: throughput[anchor] / throughput[GPU]; rows of one GPU (different hosts) pooled by geometric mean
measurements.vram_gb_at_most_note: the run completed with batch 640 on 80 GB cards, so the peak is at most 80 GB; Lambda's batch sizes grow with card memory, so the peak is likely close to the card size; this bound does not check an underestimate
